Simulation-based exploration approach:

- Bret Victor
- Richard Feyman

Baking in solution is risky. It can payoff big time (the only way to learn
programming and algorithmic thinking is to study other people's code), but it
can also backfire (blind copy-pasting).

The statistics and concepts might be very simple but this is an advantage --
newbies learn about new statistics and their features, experts can use
simulations to dig even deeper.

Even people who did the short crashcourse will learn enough (three hours of
rushing was a bad idea and I stopped teaching that short tutorial completely
even at UCPH).


There's a lot of text. If you struggle with too much text on the screen, the **bold text** always indicates a concrete, actionable task to do in a given exercise.

The primary goal is teach you skills by means of demonstration, utilizing popgen concepts as a vehicle for doing this (while also hopefully teaching you things w.r.t. those concepts you might have not thought about before).

Use `?help_pages` often.

The bare-minimum practical computational knowledge for modern popgen.


The exercises are simple on purpose:

1. not to lose people newer in popgen
2. allow the computation/simulation side stand out clearly, without being bogged down by math too much

If we're successful, this will give you the tools to comprehend the theory much more
efficiently once it comes down to using it in your research.


Good programming is in large part about keeping track of growing complexity of our scripts,
always keeping this manageable and tidy. Every bit of code should be in our script for a reason,
and ideally with comments.
